sentence: **0.4** The Holocaust is defined by USHMM as "the systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews by the Nazi German regime and its allies and collaborators."[^9] Robert Gerwarth and Stephan Malinowski state the field's position on its causes: the standard accounts of Nazi anti-Jewish policy, by Longerich, Browning and Friedländer, give no colonial causation, and the large literature on German antisemitism has not found colonial racism to be an influence.[^10] Christopher Browning, on Jewish labor in the ghettos: when the advocates of production gained room, the ideological goal was "never superseded, just temporarily deferred".[^11]

sentence: Jürgen Zimmerer compares the Herero and Nama genocide of 1904–08 with Nazi rule on three axes, genocide, the "racial state" and forced labor.[^14] Gerwarth and Malinowski argue that the breach of 1904 was largely consistent with European colonial standards of its time and that the Nazi war of annihilation broke with colonial traditions.[^15] Andreas Eckert, in a closing chapter reviewed by Mohamed Adhikari, is "quite clear that there was no direct path 'from Windhoek to Auschwitz'."[^16] (c) Colonial causation of the murder of the Jews is largely rejected (0.4).[^10] The continuity school's common ancestor is Hannah Arendt; Gerwarth and Malinowski title their critique "Hannah Arendt's Ghosts".[^10]

sentence: **4.2** Hachtmann applies war Fordism from 1933: "The term 'war Fordism' – as a special form of Fordism – will thus be used here for the years starting in 1933, in the first place because the economy of the Third Reich stood under a bellicose sign from the very beginning and made rearmament a top priority, and second because prior to 1939–1945 certain social conceptions often associated with the slogan 'Fordism' – in particular the establishment of a mass consumer society – were not central goals".[^19] The production form preceded the camp labor that entered it.

title: The Colony Enters the Factory: War Fordism, Racial Labor Hierarchy, and the Industrialization of Conquest (EA-NOUN-VERB-02 v1.0)
sentence: **5.1** Herbert names the contradiction from which the labor order grew: "the contradiction between the economic interest in exploiting as many foreigners as possible and the ideological principles of National Socialism, which sought to protect the Volk from mixing with 'foreign blood.' From this contradiction there developed a rigidly hierarchical racist system for the treatment of forced laborers."[^7] With the Poles, the first large intake, "It was possible to bring a large number of Polish workers to Germany against their will within a short time as well as to put in place a two-tiered society based on a hierarchy of 'racial' criteria."[^44] By 1944 "the four-tiered staggered wage system continued to reinforce the privileged position of German workers."[^31]
